name: Dulaglutide
lead: Dulaglutide (brand name Trulicity) is a once-weekly injectable GLP-1 receptor agonist made by Eli Lilly for type 2 diabetes. It is built from a GLP-1 peptide fused to a fragment of a human IgG4 antibody, which extends its duration of action so that a single injection lasts a week.[1] The FDA approved it in September 2014 and the EU in November 2014.[1]

Beyond glucose control, it is labelled to reduce major cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease or multiple risk factors, based on the REWIND trial.[2][3][4] It also causes modest weight loss, which is how it connects to body composition and appearance goals, but it is not approved for weight management; semaglutide and tirzepatide are the GLP-1-class drugs labelled for obesity.[1][12] The US label carries a boxed warning on thyroid C-cell tumors seen in rodents.[4]

In online fat-loss discussions it appears mostly as the lower-profile, older member of the GLP-1 family, mentioned by forum users comparing the price and availability of weekly GLP-1 pens.[20] Published research on dulaglutide centres on diabetes, cardiovascular and kidney outcomes, with head-to-head comparisons against semaglutide, liraglutide and tirzepatide.[5][9][13]
infobox: GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 fused to human IgG4 Fc)[1]

paras: Approved uses are glycemic control in adults and children 10 and older with type 2 diabetes, as an adjunct to diet and exercise, and cardiovascular risk reduction in adults with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease or risk factors.[4] It is not indicated for type 1 diabetes or diabetic ketoacidosis, and it can be used alone or alongside metformin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones or insulin.[1] It has been used widely: in 2023 it was the 63rd most prescribed medication in the US, with more than 10 million prescriptions.[1]

Weight loss is a secondary effect rather than a labelled indication. In the phase 3 program the lower doses produced average weight loss of a few kilograms, and the higher 3.0 and 4.5 mg doses slightly more.[1] Reviews of the class note that all GLP-1 agonists share a mechanism of reduced calorie intake and body weight, though the size of the effect differs by drug.[6][12]

In phase 3 trials, the 0.75 and 1.5 mg doses reduced HbA1c by about 1 percentage point, with average weight loss of around 5 pounds; the 3.0 and 4.5 mg doses, approved in 2020 on the basis of the AWARD-11 trial, reduced HbA1c by closer to 1.5 points with slightly greater weight loss.[1] Six trials involving 3,342 people supported the original approval, and the AWARD program also compared dulaglutide with metformin, sitagliptin, exenatide and liraglutide.[1][9][18]

Head-to-head, semaglutide produced larger reductions in HbA1c and weight than dulaglutide in SUSTAIN 7, and tirzepatide has outperformed semaglutide in weight and HbA1c in randomised trials, according to a 2026 narrative review.[5][12] A phase 3 trial in Chinese adults compared the dual agonist mazdutide with dulaglutide as the active comparator.[17]

In REWIND, 9,901 people with type 2 diabetes, about two-thirds without prior cardiovascular events, received dulaglutide or placebo for a median of 5.4 years; major adverse cardiovascular events fell by about 12 percent (hazard ratio 0.88).[1][2] A meta-analysis of GLP-1 agonist cardiovascular trials and a 2025 analysis of 21 trials covering 99,599 patients examine cardiovascular and safety outcomes across the class.[3][16]

Common effects are gastrointestinal: nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, dyspepsia and abdominal pain, along with decreased appetite.[1] A 2026 comparative study examined gastrointestinal safety of dulaglutide, semaglutide and tirzepatide in adults with type 2 diabetes.[14] Small increases in heart rate and small drops in systolic blood pressure have been reported.[1]

Warnings and precautions on the label include pancreatitis, hypoglycemia when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas, kidney injury and hypersensitivity reactions.[1][4] The boxed warning notes a dose- and duration-related increase in thyroid C-cell tumors in rats; whether the drug causes these tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma, in humans is unknown, and the drug is contraindicated with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2.[4] Limited data are insufficient to determine pregnancy risk, and animal studies suggest possible fetal risk.[4]

Dulaglutide is a human GLP-1 receptor agonist with about 90 percent sequence homology to native GLP-1(7-37).[4] Receptor activation raises cAMP in pancreatic beta cells, increasing glucose-dependent insulin release; it also lowers glucagon, slows gastric emptying and reduces appetite.[1][4][6]

Native GLP-1 is degraded within minutes, which is why long-acting analogues were developed; dulaglutide's antibody fragment slows clearance so that it is dosed weekly.[6][1] Grokipedia gives a half-life of about five days.[21] The medication is supplied as a prefilled single-dose pen.[1]

GLP-1 receptor agonists began with exenatide, first approved for type 2 diabetes in 2005 as a twice-daily injection; later agents extended dosing to once daily and then once weekly, including dulaglutide, albiglutide and semaglutide.[6] Dulaglutide was approved by the FDA in September 2014 with a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy focused on pancreatitis and thyroid cancer, and by the EU that November.[1] The higher 3.0 and 4.5 mg doses were approved in 2020, and the cardiovascular indication followed REWIND in 2019 and 2020.[1][2] In 2025 the SURPASS-CVOT trial showed cardiovascular non-inferiority of tirzepatide compared with dulaglutide.[12][13]

REWIND, a randomized placebo-controlled trial in type 2 diabetes, tested effects on major adverse cardiovascular events.[2] A meta-analysis of GLP-1 agonist cardiovascular outcome trials examined cardiovascular, mortality and kidney outcomes across the class.[3] Exploratory REWIND analyses examined renal outcomes, AWARD-7 compared it with insulin glargine in chronic kidney disease, AWARD-6 with liraglutide, AWARD-1 with exenatide, and SUSTAIN 7 with semaglutide.[5][7][8][9][18]

A 2025 meta-analysis of GLP-1-based therapies including dulaglutide in fatty liver disease reported reductions in liver fat across 25 randomised trials.[15] Dulaglutide served as the active comparator in the phase 2 trial of the dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist tirzepatide and in a phase 3 trial of mazdutide.[17][19]
Registered trials cover pediatric type 2 diabetes at higher doses, liver fat in diabetes with fatty liver disease, and intracranial atherosclerosis.[10][11][22]

Trulicity has been advertised directly to consumers in the US, a point a T Nation forum user raised in a thread about animal studies and drug development.[23] In a 2021 T Nation thread on appetite suppressants and fat-loss agents, a European user compared the cost of Trulicity pens with those of semaglutide, calling both expensive.[20] Lilly's sales of Trulicity were a topic of financial news coverage in 2019.[24]

Higher 3.0 and 4.5 mg doses approved; cardiovascular indication announced.[1]

lore.intro: Dulaglutide features in fat-loss forums mainly as a point of comparison with semaglutide and other weekly GLP-1 drugs.[20]

claims.claim: Trulicity is a cheaper or easier-to-get alternative to Ozempic for fat loss.
claims.believers: A forum user in 2021 compared euro prices of Trulicity and Ozempic pens and noted both were costly where he lived.[20]
claims.experts: Dulaglutide is approved for type 2 diabetes, not weight management; in SUSTAIN 7 semaglutide lowered weight and HbA1c more than dulaglutide.[4][5]

card.summary: Weekly GLP-1 diabetes drug with proven cardiovascular benefit and modest weight loss; not approved for obesity.
card.note: Boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors (rodents).

quick.overview:
Dulaglutide is a once-weekly GLP-1 injection for type 2 diabetes. It lowers blood sugar, reduced cardiovascular events in the REWIND trial and causes modest weight loss.

A head-to-head trial found semaglutide produced larger weight and HbA1c reductions.
quick.mechanism: It activates GLP-1 receptors, raising insulin release when glucose is high, slowing stomach emptying and reducing appetite.
quick.risks: Common effects are nausea and diarrhea. A boxed warning covers thyroid C-cell tumors in rats; pancreatitis is also warned. Prescription-only.

chain: Weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist injection prescribed for type 2 diabetes
Slows gastric emptying and reduces appetite
Lower calorie intake and a few kilograms of weight loss
Leaner body composition as a side effect of treatment
angle.text: Dulaglutide is prescribed to control blood sugar, and weight loss of a few kilograms is a recognised secondary effect of the drug. People interested in fat loss mostly look to the newer, higher-potency GLP-1 drugs, but dulaglutide is part of the same family and the same mechanism.
